extracted.intended_audience: appellate lawyers, agency counsel, contractors, and litigants involved in reverse FOIA (disclosure-prevention) litigation
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and criteria for deciding whether documents submitted to federal agencies by contractors (or other third parties) may be disclosed under the FOIA, 18 U.S.C. § 1905, related agency regulations (e.g., OFCC 41 C.F.R. § 60-40.*), and the proper scope/procedure of judicial review in reverse FOIA cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency regulation authorization under 5 U.S.C. § 301
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether regulations promulgated pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 301 constitute 'authorization by law' such that disclosures made pursuant to those regulations are not 'to any extent not authorized by law' for purposes of 18 U.S.C. § 1905.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuits are split: the Third Circuit upheld that §301-based disclosure regs can authorize disclosures (rendering §1905 inoperative for those disclosures), while the D.C. Circuit (Charles River Park) concluded Section 301 does not authorize regulations limiting the scope of §1905. The page urges review to resolve the conflict and notes legislative history and sponsor statements bearing on the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation and scope of 18 U.S.C. § 1905
rubrics_metrics.description: § 1905 is a criminal provision that prohibits government employees from disclosing certain types of documents 'to any extent not authorized by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because §1905 imposes criminal penalties, any claim of 'authorization by law' for disclosure must be scrutinized; allowing agencies to self-authorize by regulation would risk enabling officials to exculpate themselves from criminal liability by promulgating broad disclosure rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether §1905 is an Exemption 3 statute under FOIA
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 1905 qualifies as an Exemption 3 statute (a statute that specifically exempts information from disclosure under FOIA, 5 U.S.C. § 552(b)(3)), thereby making disclosure prohibited 'by statute' within Exemption 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circuits disagree: Westinghouse found §1905 an Exemption 3 statute; Charles River Park held it is not. The decision is characterized as a 'threshold question' in reverse FOIA cases involving confidential commercial information and affects whether documents whose disclosure would violate §1905 are exempt under Exemption 3.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to de novo judicial review in reverse FOIA actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a submitter seeking to enjoin disclosure in a reverse FOIA action is entitled to a de novo judicial determination of whether the information is exempt from disclosure (as if the government had been sued to compel disclosure), or whether review is limited to the Administrative Procedure Act's record-review standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several circuits (D.C. Circuit, Fourth Circuit and others) have held submitters are entitled to de novo review; the court below held review limited to APA §706 (arbitrary, capricious or abuse of discretion review). The page argues that because FOIA protections are implicated and agencies often fail to develop adequate records, de novo review is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied private cause of action under Exemption 4 and/or §1905
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a private party (submitter) may have an implied equitable cause of action to enjoin disclosure under Exemption 4 (confidential commercial information) and/or 18 U.S.C. § 1905.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some courts have implied such a cause of action (and thereby permitted de novo equitable relief); other courts (e.g., the Third Circuit) have rejected the implication. The page suggests courts have applied Cort v. Ash inconsistently when deciding whether to imply a cause of action.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFCC public-disclosure balancing test (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.2(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: OFCC regulations provide: 'upon the request of any person for identifiable records obtained or generated pursuant to Executive Order 11246 ... such records shall be made available for inspection and copying ... if it is determined that the requested inspection or copying furthers the public interest and does not impede any of the functions of the OFCC or the Compliance Agencies except in the case of records disclosure of which is prohibited by law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure therefore requires a public-interest showing and an assessment whether disclosure would impede agency functions; the regulation contains an explicit exception where disclosure is prohibited by law.

rubrics_metrics.name: OFCC 'blanket waiver' principle re: FOIA exemptions
rubrics_metrics.description: OFCC rules include a provision effectively waiving resistance to disclosure of records falling within FOIA exemption categories if disclosure is found to further the public interest and not impede agency functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulations create a policy favoring disclosure to aid elimination of employment discrimination, subject to the public-interest/impairment test and statutory prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: FOIA exemptions (enumeration under 5 U.S.C. § 552(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress identified nine categories of information exempt from mandatory disclosure under FOIA (e.g., national defense/classified, internal personnel rules, statutes requiring nondisclosure, trade secrets/confidential commercial information, inter/intra-agency memoranda, personnel/medical files, law-enforcement investigatory records, financial institution reports, geological/geophysical data).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated exemptions are the statutory baseline for withholding decisions; agency regulations (e.g., OFCC) interact with these exemptions in defining disclosure obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for portions of AAP revealing 'major shifts or changes' (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.3(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Those portions of affirmative action plans (goals and timetables) that would be confidential commercial or financial information because they indicate, and only to the extent that they indicate, that a contractor plans major shifts or changes in his personnel requirements and he has not made this information available to the public, should be withheld.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An agency determination to withhold this type of information 'should be made only after receiving verification and a satisfactory explanation from the contractor that the information should be withheld.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for staffing patterns and pay scales in AAPs (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.3(a)(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Portions of affirmative action plans constituting information on staffing patterns and pay scales are exempt to the extent release would injure the business or financial position of the contractor, would release confidential financial information of an employee, or would be an unwarranted invasion of employee privacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The withholding decision must assess likely injury to the contractor or employees and is limited to the portions that would cause such harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for names of individual complainants (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.3(a)(3))
rubrics_metrics.description: The names of individual complainants in compliance files are identified as a category that should be withheld from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects privacy and potentially safety of complainants; treated as a specific subcategory for nondisclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for assignment-of-officers information (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.3(a)(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments to particular contractors of named compliance officers should be withheld where disclosure would subject the named compliance officers to undue harassment or would affect the efficient enforcement of the Executive Order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recognizes secrecy needs for enforcement personnel and balances disclosure against harassment/enforcement efficiency concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for compliance investigation files during active review or enforcement (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.3(a)(5))
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance investigation files including the standard compliance review report and related documents are exempt during the course of the review or while enforcement action is in progress or contemplated, but only to the extent that information therein constitutes trade secrets/confidential commercial or financial information, inter/intra-agency memoranda not available in litigation, personnel/medical files, informant-privileged data, or information prohibited by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision treats active investigatory materials as particularly sensitive and links withholding to specific FOIA-type exemptions and privileges; it also reflects the regulatory view that such files may be 'investigatory records' under FOIA Exemption 7 in some contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exemption for preemployment selection tests (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.3(a)(6))
rubrics_metrics.description: Copies of preemployment selection tests used by contractors are listed as a category to be withheld from disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protects integrity of testing instruments and prevents gaming of selection processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: EEO-1 report disclosure policy (41 C.F.R. § 60-40.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Standard Form 100 (EEO-1), submitted by contractors, 'shall be disclosed pending further instructions from the Director, OFCC,' notwithstanding that EEOC (which also collects EEO-1 data) is statutorily prohibited from disclosing EEO-1 reports in its possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OFCC's rule distinguishes OFCC custody from EEOC custody and directs disclosure of EEO-1 data unless revised by the Director.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative appeal timing and 'investigatory file' treatment (41 C.F.R. § 60-60.4(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Contractors should identify allegedly non-disclosable information; the Contract Compliance Officer decides within 10 days; the contractor may appeal to the Director of OFCC within 10 days; Director must decide within 10 days. However, during a compliance review or while enforcement action is in progress or contemplated, information obtained from a contractor is to be considered part of an investigatory file and treated as exempt under FOIA during the compliance review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The FOIA statutory 10-day substantive-decision limit can force agencies to disclose before appeal is resolved; the regulation explicitly classifies certain compliance materials as investigatory for withholding purposes during active review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of verification and satisfactory explanation from contractor for withholding
rubrics_metrics.description: For certain categories (e.g., AAP portions indicating planned major personnel shifts), the agency should withhold only 'after receiving verification and a satisfactory explanation from the contractor that the information should be withheld.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places evidentiary burden on contractor to justify confidentiality for specific sensitive information when seeking nondisclosure under the OFCC rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural standard: district court hearing to determine exemption (de novo-equivalent process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a plaintiff challenges disclosure, the district court should 'hold a hearing to determine whether the information involved here would have been exempt just as it would if a suit had been brought under the FOIA to compel disclosure' — i.e., make a threshold de novo determination of disclosability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard, invoked by the D.C. Circuit, treats reverse FOIA plaintiffs as entitled to the same factual and legal determination a FOIA requester would receive, and supports a trial-like proceeding rather than mere record review in some circuits.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA §706 'record review' vs de novo factfinding distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Administrative Procedure Act, judicial review ordinarily is limited to 'a review of the whole (agency) record or parts of it cited by a party' (5 U.S.C. § 706), which is an 'arbitrary and capricious' standard, contrasted with the de novo review some circuits require in reverse FOIA cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether APA-limited review controls or de novo review is required determines the scope of judicial factfinding and relief; the page documents circuit splits and urges Supreme Court resolution because of practical consequences for submitters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical constraints justifying de novo review (notice, FOIA time limits, lack of agency findings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical features of the FOIA and agency process—lack of statutory or regulatory notice to submitters, gratuitous or inadequate notice when provided, the FOIA's ten-day substantive decision time limit, and the frequent absence of agency findings—make meaningful judicial review based on the agency record difficult.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factual realities are presented as policy and practical reasons supporting de novo judicial determination of disclosability for submitters threatened with disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public-policy concern against allowing agencies to self-exempt from criminal prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: Permitting agencies or agency officials to define or redefine the scope of illegal conduct under §1905 by promulgating disclosure regulations would allow them to avoid criminal liability for disclosures that otherwise would violate §1905.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court should avoid construing statutes/regulations so as to permit executive self-exemption from criminal statutes; this is presented as an argument against treating §301 regulations as sufficient 'authorization by law' for purposes of §1905.
